title: handle gcfg struct tags when reading environment variables
description:
The gcfg.ReadInto function handles gcfg struct tags, but we need to use them when reading environment variables (when present). This gcfgTagOrStructName() function will return a gcfg tag or fall back to the field.Name if no such struct tag is present. It also replaces dashes by underscores to follow env var and field naming conventions.


As an aside:

Reading here: https://pkg.go.dev/gopkg.in/gcfg.v1#hdr-Data_structure

> The mapping of each section or variable name to fields is done either based on the "gcfg" struct tag or by matching the name of the section or variable, ignoring case. In the latter case, hyphens '-' in section and variable names correspond to underscores '_' in field names.

I suspect this means that our test case is proper and the `another-name` struct tag _should_ be overridden by the `ANOTHER_NAME` env var. However, I wanted to be sure, since the "former" case (of a gcfg struct tag) does _not_ seem to follow the convention of replacing dashes by underscores. 

Close #1

title: Set properties of embedded structs, slices in subsections, and defined types
description:
Some properties a configuration file exposes normally could not be set by an environment variable at all, and two shapes of property took the calling process down at startup rather than being ignored.

Found while writing end-to-end tests for Package Manager, where `PACKAGEMANAGER_OPENIDCONNECT_ISSUER` silently did nothing and the server started with no OpenID Connect provider configured (rstudio/package-manager#20160).

## The defects

**The walker only went one field deep.** For an anonymous embedded struct it looked for the embedded type's own name, found nothing, and moved on, discarding a variable that named a real property without a word. The same applied to a *section* declared on a struct embedded in the config, since gcfg resolves a section name by promotion too.

**Setting a slice property of a subsection panicked.** Both map branches called `reflect.Value.Elem` on the slice itself:

```
panic: reflect: call of reflect.Value.Elem on slice Value
```

The plain-section branch never had this bug. No test covered a slice inside a subsection, which is how it survived.

**Setting a property of a defined type with a basic underlying kind panicked**, because the parsed value had the underlying type, which is not assignable to the defined type:

```
panic: reflect.Set: value of type string is not assignable to type config.AccessLogFormat
```

**A `gcfg` tag carrying options was unreachable.** `fieldToEnvVar` uppercased the whole tag, so `gcfg:"the-number,int=dho"` produced the name `THE_NUMBER,INT=DHO`, which no environment variable can have. Making it reachable meant honouring the `int=` option too, or the same field would read 511 from a file and 777 from a variable.

**An environment-only subsection could get the wrong key.** The property name was removed by replacing its first occurrence rather than trimming the end, so `SEC_PROD_URL_v2_URL` created a subsection called `PROD_v2_URL`.

## The intended contract

I established this by testing gcfg rather than by reading it, having got it wrong the first time. An embedded struct is reachable **both** ways:

* its fields are addressable as though declared on the outer struct; and
* the embedded struct itself is addressable by its type name, which is what makes an embedded `time.Time` work.

Embedding an *unexported* type is the exception: reflect will not set the field, and gcfg drops candidates it cannot set, so only its promoted fields are reachable. Crucially the unexported field must not occupy the name either, or it cancels a real field that shares it.

Shadowing follows Go's promotion rules, and gcfg's integer bases are matched, including the per-field `int=` override.

## Verification

The suite is 31 tests, up from 11, and runs under Go 1.17 (the version go.mod declares) as well as current Go.

`parity_test.go` is a differential test against gcfg itself, since gcfg is the only trustworthy oracle for what a name means. It generates every name that could plausibly address something from reflection — deliberately without consulting the code under test — and requires that a name gcfg accepts produce the same result from the environment, and that a name gcfg refuses not quietly set something. Measured against each state of this branch:

| version | divergences |
| --- | --- |
| v0.2.1 | 13 |
| first commit | 9 |
| second commit | 9 |
| third commit | 5 |
| now | 0 |

Against Package Manager's real configuration, probing all 493 properties end to end: 439 reachable before, 493 after.

## Behavior change for callers

Variables that were previously ignored will start taking effect on upgrade. `posit-dev/connect`, `rstudio/chronicle`, `rstudio/chronicle-agent` and `rstudio/package-manager` all pin v0.2.1 today. In Package Manager this makes 20 properties reachable, including `OpenIDConnect.Issuer` and every property of an identity federation provider. Also worth knowing before bumping:

* a defined integer type now accepts octal, so `0777` becomes 511 where it was 777;
* an environment-only subsection whose key ends in a property name gets a different key than before.

Five divergences from gcfg remain, listed in the README. Each needs a piece of gcfg's setter machinery this package does not reproduce, and none has a caller today.

## Note on the CI matrix

The matrix built `stable` and `oldstable` only, so it never built the Go version go.mod declares, and a use of a newer standard library function passed CI while breaking anyone on 1.17. It now builds 1.17 explicitly. Since 1.17 has been out of support since 2022, raising the floor instead may be preferable — that affects consumers, so it is not done here.

title: Report which environment variables were applied and which were not
description:
Stacked on #13. Review #11, #12 and #13 first.

A caller has no way to tell which environment variables took effect. A misspelled one, such as `APP_SERVER_ADRESS`, does nothing and goes unnoticed, though gcfg warns about the same mistake in a file. A caller that wants to warn about such variables, or log which ones configured it, needs to know. This answers #4, with a returned report instead of the callback proposed there.

## Before and after

```sh
APP_SERVER_ADRESS=http://x     # typo
APP_SERVER_ADDRESS=http://y
APP_API_KEY=abc                # not a setting: there is no API section
```

```
v0.3.0:  "Server":{"Address":"http://y"}   (the typo is ignored, and the caller can't tell)
this PR: "Server":{"Address":"http://y"}
         Applied: ["APP_SERVER_ADDRESS"]
         Unused:  ["APP_SERVER_ADRESS"]
```

<details>
<summary>How the output above was produced</summary>

A small program, run once against v0.3.0 and once against this branch:

```go
// Duration parses with time.ParseDuration.
type Duration time.Duration

func (d *Duration) UnmarshalText(b []byte) error {
	v, err := time.ParseDuration(string(b))
	*d = Duration(v)
	return err
}

func (d Duration) MarshalText() ([]byte, error) { return []byte(time.Duration(d).String()), nil }

// Common holds options shared by several sections, and is embedded in each.
type Common struct {
	Mode        bool
	ModeTimeout Duration
}

type Config struct {
	Server struct {
		Address string
	}
	Auth struct {
		Common
	}
	Backend map[string]*struct {
		Logging bool
	}
}
```

```go
var cfg Config
err := gcfgenv.ReadWithEnvInto(strings.NewReader(""), "APP", &cfg)
// this PR, for the report:
report, err := gcfgenv.ReadWithEnvIntoReport(strings.NewReader(""), "APP", &cfg)
```

There is no config file, so everything comes from the environment. JSON output is trimmed to the section shown.

</details>

Two new functions sit alongside the existing ones:

```go
type Report struct {
	Applied []string // set a field; sorted
	Unused  []string // named a section but set nothing; sorted
}

func ReadWithEnvIntoReport(r io.Reader, envPrefix string, config interface{}) (Report, error)
func ReadFileWithEnvIntoReport(filename, envPrefix string, config interface{}) (Report, error)
```

- **Applied** is every variable that set a field.
- **Unused** is every variable that starts with the prefix, a section's name and `_` but set nothing. A variable that carries the prefix but names no section is left out, because the prefix is not reserved for settings: an application may set prefixed variables of its own, and Kubernetes adds `<SERVICE>_PORT_*`. `Unused` is nil when there is no prefix.
- A section declared as a pointer to a struct is not set from the environment, so its variables appear in neither list.
- A `Report` holds names only, never values.
- On a fatal error the report is empty. With only gcfg's non-fatal warnings it is complete, and `gcfg.FatalOnly(err)` returns nil. The README explains how to tell the two apart.

`ReadWithEnvInto` and `ReadFileWithEnvInto` keep their signatures and errors. They are thin wrappers that discard the report, so nothing changes for a caller that does not opt in. Applied names are collected in a set passed through `setGcfgWithEnvMap`, with no package state.

## Verification

- `TestReport` covers a plain field, an existing subsection, a new subsection, the unnamed subsection, a `Default_*` section, a tag-renamed section, unknown names in plain and map sections, and an unparseable embedded type name. It also covers four names that must be absent: a prefixed name under no section, a bare section name, the Go name of a renamed section, and a name without the prefix.
- `TestReportWithOverlappingSectionNames` covers `Sec` next to `Sec_X`, `TestReportThroughAnEmbeddedStruct` a section promoted from an embedded struct, and `TestReportSkipsPointerSections` a pointer section.
- `TestReportWithoutAPrefix`, `TestReportOnError`, `TestReportWithUpstreamWarnings` and `TestReportFromTheProcessEnvironment` cover the rest of the contract, including both public functions.
- `make`, `make test` (47 tests, 98.6% coverage) and `make check` pass.

title: Set the unnamed subsection when a variable has no subsection name
description:
Stacked on #12. Review #11 and #12 first.

For a map-valued section, a variable that leaves out the subsection name, such as `APP_SEC_FIELD`, was dropped unless the unnamed subsection already existed. In a file, `[sec]` with `field = x` creates that subsection. So the same variable worked for a section whose unnamed subsection the application seeds in its defaults, and was silently discarded for one that it doesn't.

## Before and after

```sh
APP_BACKEND_LOGGING=true    # same as [Backend] Logging = true in a file
```

```
v0.3.0:  "Backend":null                      (the variable is dropped, no error)
this PR: "Backend":{"":{"Logging":true}}
```

The named form, `APP_BACKEND_MAIN_LOGGING=true`, gives `"Backend":{"MAIN":{"Logging":true}}` both before and after.

<details>
<summary>How the output above was produced</summary>

A small program, run once against v0.3.0 and once against this branch:

```go
// Duration parses with time.ParseDuration.
type Duration time.Duration

func (d *Duration) UnmarshalText(b []byte) error {
	v, err := time.ParseDuration(string(b))
	*d = Duration(v)
	return err
}

func (d Duration) MarshalText() ([]byte, error) { return []byte(time.Duration(d).String()), nil }

// Common holds options shared by several sections, and is embedded in each.
type Common struct {
	Mode        bool
	ModeTimeout Duration
}

type Config struct {
	Server struct {
		Address string
	}
	Auth struct {
		Common
	}
	Backend map[string]*struct {
		Logging bool
	}
}
```

```go
var cfg Config
err := gcfgenv.ReadWithEnvInto(strings.NewReader(""), "APP", &cfg)
```

There is no config file, so everything comes from the environment. JSON output is trimmed to the section shown.

</details>

**Behavior change.** A variable of this form that was ignored before now takes effect, and a value that fails to parse now fails the read. The v0.4.0 release notes will call this out.

The key for a new subsection comes from trimming `_<PROPERTY>` off the end of the variable, which can never match a variable that is just `<PROPERTY>`. A third pass now runs after the keyed one. A leftover variable that exactly equals a property name creates or fills the unnamed subsection, taking the `Default_*` values the way the keyed pass does.

Because it runs last, a variable that resolved before still resolves the same way. With properties `A_B` and `B`, `SEC_A_B` stays property `B` of subsection `A`.

A related case predates this PR: when one property's name ends in another's, as with `Other_Field` and `Field`, the property declared first claims `SEC_K_OTHER_FIELD`. The README now says so, and a test pins it.

## Verification

- `TestUnnamedSubsection` compares the result with `gcfg.ReadStringInto` for `[sec]`, including defaults, alongside a named subsection, and with a seeded unnamed subsection.
- `TestUnnamedSubsectionDoesNotOverrideAKey` covers the `A_B` / `B` case.
- `TestOverlappingPropertyNamesFollowDeclarationOrder` covers the `Other_Field` / `Field` case in both declaration orders.
- `parityKeys` now includes `""`, so `TestParityWithGcfgAcrossShapes` compares the unnamed form against `[sec]` for every map shape. With the source change reverted, it fails for every one of them.
- `make`, `make test` and `make check` pass.

title: Ignore an embedded struct's type name unless its type parses from text
description:
Stacked on #11. Review that one first.

An exported embedded struct is addressable by its type name, so that an embedded `time.Time` can be set. For any other struct, a variable naming the type always failed the read with `unsupported type: struct`, even though nothing could ever be set that way. An application that embeds a shared options struct in its sections could be stopped at startup by a variable that happens to match the type's name.

## Before and after

`[Auth]` embeds a `Common` struct, so `COMMON` is a valid type name but not a setting.

```sh
APP_AUTH_COMMON=x
```

```
v0.3.0:  unsupported type: struct        (the read fails)
this PR: no error, the variable sets nothing
```

The promoted fields still work: `APP_AUTH_MODETIMEOUT=7m` gives `"ModeTimeout":"7m0s"` both before and after.

<details>
<summary>How the output above was produced</summary>

A small program, run once against v0.3.0 and once against this branch:

```go
// Duration parses with time.ParseDuration.
type Duration time.Duration

func (d *Duration) UnmarshalText(b []byte) error {
	v, err := time.ParseDuration(string(b))
	*d = Duration(v)
	return err
}

func (d Duration) MarshalText() ([]byte, error) { return []byte(time.Duration(d).String()), nil }

// Common holds options shared by several sections, and is embedded in each.
type Common struct {
	Mode        bool
	ModeTimeout Duration
}

type Config struct {
	Server struct {
		Address string
	}
	Auth struct {
		Common
	}
	Backend map[string]*struct {
		Logging bool
	}
}
```

```go
var cfg Config
err := gcfgenv.ReadWithEnvInto(strings.NewReader(""), "APP", &cfg)
```

There is no config file, so everything comes from the environment. JSON output is trimmed to the section shown.

</details>

`flatField` gains a `settable` flag. It is false for an exported embedded struct, or pointer to one, whose type does not implement `encoding.TextUnmarshaler`, and the property loops skip such a field, so the variable is simply unused. An embedded pointer to a struct (`*Common`) failed the same way and gets the same treatment; its promoted fields are still unreachable, as the README already says. Two things stay as they were:

- **Name resolution.** The name still takes part in shadowing and ambiguity, as it does in gcfg, which resolves it with `FieldByNameFunc` and only filters on `CanSet`. A deeper field of the same name stays hidden.
- **Sections.** At the top level, gcfg treats an exported embedded struct as a valid section (`TestEmbeddedSections`), so the flag only applies to properties.

gcfg itself accepts the name in a file and then fails to parse it. The README lists that as a remaining difference.

## Verification

- `TestEmbeddedStructByTypeNameNeedsAParseableType` covers a plain section, an existing subsection and a subsection created from the environment. The type name is ignored, and the promoted field is still set.
- `TestEmbeddedPointerByTypeName` covers an embedded pointer, both to a type that parses from text and to one that does not, and compares the result with gcfg.
- `TestEmbeddedParseableStructByTypeName` covers a text-parseable struct other than `time.Time`, embedded by value, against gcfg.
- `TestUnparseableEmbeddedTypeNameStillShadows` checks that shadowing is unchanged.
- `TestEmbeddedStructByTypeName`, `TestEmbeddedStructs`, the `TestUnexportedEmbedded*` tests, `TestEmbeddedSections` and `TestParityWithGcfgAcrossShapes` pass without edits.
- With the source change reverted, `TestEmbeddedStructByTypeNameNeedsAParseableType`, `TestUnparseableEmbeddedTypeNameStillShadows` and `TestEmbeddedPointerByTypeName` fail.
- `make`, `make test` and `make check` pass.

title: Name the environment variable in a parse error
description:
A value that fails to parse fails the read, as it does in a file, but the error gave no hint of which variable held it. With many variables set, the only way to find the bad one was to check each by hand.

## Before and after

```sh
APP_AUTH_MODETIMEOUT=30    # a duration with no unit
```

```
v0.3.0:  time: missing unit in duration "30"
this PR: environment variable APP_AUTH_MODETIMEOUT: time: missing unit in duration "30"
```

<details>
<summary>How the output above was produced</summary>

A small program, run once against v0.3.0 and once against this branch:

```go
// Duration parses with time.ParseDuration.
type Duration time.Duration

func (d *Duration) UnmarshalText(b []byte) error {
	v, err := time.ParseDuration(string(b))
	*d = Duration(v)
	return err
}

func (d Duration) MarshalText() ([]byte, error) { return []byte(time.Duration(d).String()), nil }

// Common holds options shared by several sections, and is embedded in each.
type Common struct {
	Mode        bool
	ModeTimeout Duration
}

type Config struct {
	Server struct {
		Address string
	}
	Auth struct {
		Common
	}
	Backend map[string]*struct {
		Logging bool
	}
}
```

```go
var cfg Config
err := gcfgenv.ReadWithEnvInto(strings.NewReader(""), "APP", &cfg)
```

There is no config file, so everything comes from the environment. JSON output is trimmed to the section shown.

</details>

`setField` now takes the variable's full name, including the prefix, and wraps the error. The original error stays wrapped, so `errors.Unwrap` and `errors.As` still reach it.

This is the first of four stacked PRs for gcfgenv v0.4.0. Review them in order; each later one is based on the one before.

## Verification

- The three existing `ErrorMatches "failed to parse.*"` assertions in `TestSections` and `TestSubsections` now match the exact variable name. Between them they cover all three call sites: a plain section, an existing subsection, and a subsection created from the environment.
- `TestErrorsNameTheVariable` adds a non-empty prefix and checks the wrapped error.
- With the source change reverted, those three tests fail.
- `make`, `make test` and `make check` pass.
